name: min-lang
desc: Small but practical concatenative programming language and shell
why: A small concatenative language that doubles as a shell, a delightfully odd corner with a real idea behind it.

brief.what_it_is: min is a functional, concatenative programming language with minimalist syntax, a small standard library, and a REPL, all packed into a single file. Programs are written as sequences of values and quotations that operate on a stack, and the language has a few data types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, dictionaries, and quotations (lists). The project's repo describes it as a language and shell. The homepage example shows it listing files modified in the last hour, so it is used for practical scripting as well as pure stack puzzles. The input is min source code or REPL input, and the output is computed values or side effects such as printed results or files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames min as a small but practical language that stays minimal in syntax and size while still being useful for everyday tasks. Its sibling mn is pitched as the even more bare-bones option for people who do not need all of min's features.
brief.how_it_works: Code is a sequence of words that push values or quotations onto a stack, and combinators such as filter and linrec consume and produce stack values. Quotations are parenthesised blocks of code, and the language is homoiconic, so code can be accessed as data. Sigils provide syntactic sugar for environment variables, quoting, and defining or binding data, and sys.pwd and fs.mtime show the namespaced standard library in use. The implementation is written in Nim and statically compiled into one file, so it can also be embedded in other Nim programs.

commands_seen.context: Homepage example (written across three lines on the page) that recursively lists all files in the current folder modified in the last hour. sys.pwd gets the current directory, sys.ls-r lists recursively, and filter keeps entries whose mtime is within 3600 seconds of time.now.
Homepage example (written across four lines on the page) that computes the factorial of 5 with the linrec combinator.
Homepage download label, not a shell command as such; it names the release version the page offers.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a download labelled 'get min v560-0' and the repo tarball and zip are version 5600 on sourcehut. Because it is a single statically compiled binary, no runtime or configuration is mentioned on the pages I read. Installation via brew is from the brew formula (executable: min); I did not find install steps beyond that in the pages fetched. No accounts or hardware are needed as far as the pages show.
brief.standout: A concatenative language with a homoiconic design, combinators for stack manipulation and dequoting, and an advanced REPL with auto-completion and history, all shipped as a single self-contained file. The homepage's first example is a one-line shell-style file finder written in the language itself, which blurs the line between language and shell.
brief.status: maintained, with caveats. The GitHub README says the project was moved to sourcehut on 2026-06-16. The sourcehut page shows its latest commits as about four months old (commits 'Update', 'Re-releasing using ConVer', and 'Formatted changelog'), and the current version is 5600 (v560-0 on the homepage). The homepage and the scout note both describe it as active, but I did not see a recent release date.
brief.caveats: The GitHub repo is now only a pointer to sourcehut, so links on the homepage may go to a moved or stale project. The homepage describes it as a language with a shell-like REPL rather than a full interactive shell, so avoid calling it a Unix shell replacement. I did not see platform or licence details beyond a GitHub licence badge, and I did not fetch the guide or NimConf talk. The tarball and zip downloads are offered from sourcehut.
quotes: min is a functional, concatenative programming language with a minimalist syntax, a small but practical standard library, and an advanced REPL. All packed in a single file.
Entirely written in Nim. It can be easily embedded in other Nim programs.
Don't need all of these features? If you are looking for something even smaller and more bare-bones, check out mn, min's even more minimalist little brother.

entry.title: min
entry.tldr: A small concatenative language with a REPL, where programs are words and quoted blocks acting on a stack, shipped as one binary.
entry.deeper_look:
min is a functional, concatenative programming language. A program is a sequence of words that push values or quotations onto a stack, and other words consume them. There are few data types: integers, floats, strings, booleans, dictionaries, and quotations, which are parenthesised lists of code. The standard library is small and namespaced, with names like `sys.pwd`, `sys.ls-r` and `fs.mtime`.

The idea underneath is concatenative programming. There are no named arguments to thread around. Functions compose by being written next to each other, and combinators such as `filter` and `linrec` take quotations off the stack and run them. Because the language is homoiconic, a quotation is both code and a list you can inspect. Once that clicks, the stack stops feeling like a puzzle and starts to feel like a pipeline.

It is also meant for everyday scripting. The homepage's first example is a one-line file finder: list the current directory recursively and keep entries modified in the last hour. The REPL has auto-completion and history, so it works as a shell-like prompt, though the project describes it as a language rather than a Unix shell replacement.

The implementation is written in Nim and compiled statically into a single file. It can be embedded in other Nim programs. A sibling called mn is the even more bare-bones version for people who do not need everything min offers.

entry.whats_unique: It is a concatenative, homoiconic language that is also practical for file-and-shell tasks, with a REPL and a standard library, all in one self-contained binary.
entry.caveats: The project moved from GitHub to sourcehut, where the latest commits are about four months old, so some links may be stale and the release cadence is unclear.
